segments.text: The last verb of the chapter — and, like Hindi's karnā and Tamil's sey, it is a "do" verb that builds a hundred others.
ജോലി (jōli, "work, job"): ജോ (jō) + ലി (li). ചെയ്യുക (ceyyuka, "do"): ചെ (ce) + യ്യു (doubled yy) + ക (ka).

ചെയ്യുക (ceyyuka, "to do, to make") is core native Dravidian — the very same root as Tamil செய் (sey, "to do"). Malayalam — like Hindi with karnā, Tamil with sey, Telugu with cēyu, Kannada with māḍu — builds compound verbs by putting a noun in front of it:
ജോലി ചെയ്യുക (jōli ceyyuka) = "work-do" = "to work" (jōli, "work").
സഹായിക്കുക (sahāyikkuka) = "to help" (Sanskrit sahāya).
So "I work" is ഞാൻ ജോലി ചെയ്യുന്നു (ñān jōli ceyyunnu) — same -unnu present, pronoun kept. Ceyyuka and Tamil's sey are, at root, one word — the Dravidian "do" that these languages all lean on.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: noun + ചെയ്യുക = a new verb

segments.text: This "noun + ceyyuka" pattern is the twin of Hindi's "noun + karnā," Tamil's "noun + sey," Telugu's "noun + cēyu," and Kannada's "noun + māḍu." Five languages, two of them from an unrelated family, all landed on the same trick.

segments.text: Your first full, moving sentence — and the language names itself after a landscape.
മലയാളം (malayāḷaṁ): മ (ma) + ല (la) + യാ (yā) + ള (retroflex ḷa) + ം (ṁ).

ഞാൻ മലയാളം സംസാരിക്കുന്നു = ഞാൻ (ñān, "I") + മലയാളം (malayāḷaṁ, the object) + സംസാരിക്കുന്നു (saṁsārikkunnu, "speak") — "I Malayalam speak," the verb last. The name മലയാളം (malayāḷaṁ) is native Dravidian: മല (mala, "mountain") + ആളം (āḷaṁ, "place, region") — "the mountain land," named for the Western Ghats along the coast where it is spoken. Its signature retroflex ള (ḷ) sits right in the middle of the word.

Because saṁsārikkunnu is the same for every person (Chapter 5's big surprise), the pronoun ഞാൻ (ñān) cannot be dropped — it is the only thing marking "I." Where Tamil would happily say just pēsugiṟēṉ, Malayalam must keep the ñān.

tāmasikkuka "to live" (Sanskrit-derived; where Tamil uses native vāḻ).
ceyyuka "to do" becomes jōli ceyyuka "to work" — the same root as Tamil sey.
malayāḷaṁ = mala "mountain" + āḷaṁ "place" — "the mountain land".

In one breath, say your language, your city, and your work in Malayalam — and note what stays the same in every verb. (Ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu. Ñān … il tāmasikkunnu. Ñān jōli ceyyunnu — the verb never changes for person.)

segments.text: So far, "to be." Here is a verb that does something — and it reveals the single strangest, simplest thing about Malayalam grammar.
സം (saṁ) + സാ (sā) + രി (ri) + ക്കുക (kkuka, doubled kk.
the -uka infinitive) becomes സംസാരിക്കുക (saṁsārikkuka).

സംസാരിക്കുക (saṁsārikkuka, "to speak, to converse") is Sanskrit-derived (from saṃsāra, "flowing together, intercourse") — one more sign of Malayalam's deep Sanskrit layer, alongside its native paṟayuka ("to say"). To say "I speak," Malayalam adds the present ending -ഉന്നു (-unnu) to the stem:
saṁsārikk- (speak) + -unnu (present) becomes സംസാരിക്കുന്നു (saṁsārikkunnu), "speak / am speaking."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the verb never changes for person

segments.text: Here is Malayalam's great surprise. In Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada the verb changes ending for who acts (pēsugiṟēṉ "I speak," pēsugiṟāṉ "he speaks"). Malayalam does not. The verb is the same for everyone:
ñān saṁsārikkunnu — "I speak".
nī saṁsārikkunnu — "you speak".
avan saṁsārikkunnu — "he speaks".

One form, all persons. Malayalam threw away person-agreement entirely — which is exactly why (Chapter 3) it can never drop the pronoun: the verb won't tell you who. Of all its Dravidian sisters, Malayalam went the furthest here.
How does the Malayalam verb change between "I speak" and "he speaks," and what does that force you to keep? (It does not change — one form for all persons; so the pronoun must always be said.)

segments.text: A second verb, so you can say where you live — and again the Sanskrit layer shows.
താ (tā) + മ (ma) + സി (si) + ക്കുക (kkuka, the -uka infinitive) becomes താമസിക്കുക (tāmasikkuka).

താമസിക്കുക (tāmasikkuka, "to live, to reside, to stay, to delay") is Sanskrit-derived (from tāmasa / tamas, "dwelling, tarrying"). Malayalam often prefers such Sanskrit-built verbs where Tamil uses a native word (vāḻ). "I live in Kochi" is ഞാൻ കൊച്ചിയിൽ താമസിക്കുന്നു (ñān kocciyil tāmasikkunnu) — again the same -unnu present, the same for every person.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: "in" comes after the noun

segments.text: കൊച്ചിയിൽ (kocciyil) = Kochi + -ഇൽ (-il, "in"), glued to the end of the noun. Malayalam uses postpositions (case-suffixes) where English uses prepositions: "Kochi-in I live," the verb last — and the pronoun kept.
